headline: Sea Bright rocks at first light: gator blues crash the bunker, fluke picks up steam in Belmar
subhead: Bluefish spilling south out of the Hook, a real fluke bite finally showing at the inlets, and the new moon building toward something worth waiting for.
body_markdown:
Quarter to six, north end of the Sea Bright rocks, and there's a guy I've never met standing on the third jetty down heaving a bunker spoon like he's trying to hit Staten Island. Turns out he had reason to. Fifteen minutes later a blitz rolled through tight to the rocks — real gator blues, eight to twelve pounds, tails white water and gulls dropping out of the sky like the ceiling fell in. He hooked up on the second cast after the spoon, lost one, landed a nine-pounder that took him halfway down the jetty chasing drag. I've fished this stretch long enough to know that when the bait's stacked this thick this close to the beach, you don't need finesse. You need to be standing there when it happens.

That blitz has been building since the gator run hit Sandy Hook proper, and it's been leaking south into our water for about a week now. Bunker pods are running tight to the beach from the Hook down through Monmouth Beach, and wherever they bunch up against structure — jetty tips, the deeper pockets off the third and fourth rocks at Sea Bright — the blues have been finding them on the tide change, both ends. Poppers work early when it's still gray out, then switch to bunker spoons or big Ava jigs once the sun's up and the fish push deeper along the rocks. I've been fishing the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, because that's when the current sets up a seam right off the tip where bait gets pinned and the blues stack up to feed on it. Don't overthink the retrieve. These fish aren't shy.

Fluke's the other story worth telling this week, and it's a better one than we've had most of the summer. Shark River Inlet and Manasquan Inlet have both been giving up better-grade fish than July, and Belmar's weigh station has had a few boats bring double-digit fluke to the scale — not a banner week, but a real uptick after a mixed-bag summer. The pattern's simple: bait's pushed shallow with the warm water, and the fluke have followed it right up into the inlet channels and the drop-offs along the jetty rocks at Manasquan. I've had my best luck drifting the deeper edge on the outgoing, 15 to 22 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's ripping and you need the extra scent to hold fish on. Slow drag, not a swim. These fish are eating close to bottom right now.

Striped bass are still doing what they've been doing all month, which is to say: present, but not stupid. We said last week the building tidal flow into this new moon would sharpen things up at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what's starting to happen. The bass I'm finding are holding tight to the rock piles at the Manasquan Inlet jetties and the deeper scour holes off Spring Lake, feeding hardest in that last hour of the ebb when the current really starts moving water off the structure. Swimmers — a Danny or a Redfin in bone or bunker pattern — worked slow along the rocks at first light have been the ticket, along with the occasional teen-class fish on a bucktail bounced through the wash at Asbury Park. Nothing's blowing up out there. It's a jetty-by-jetty grind, and you need to fish the tide, not the clock. But the pattern holds, and with the new moon on the 12th pushing more water through these inlets, I expect the current seams to sharpen up further before this week's out.

No albie signs yet, and I wasn't expecting any — we flagged this stretch as an early-arrival spot before Sandy Hook usually sees them, but that new moon trigger hasn't flipped yet. Worth watching the Manasquan Inlet rocks and the Spring Lake jetties over the next ten days, because when those fish do show, this is often where they show first on this whole stretch of coast.

Ocean's been a little beat up — better than three feet of swell running out there most of the week, which has kept some of the surf guys off the outer bars and pushed more effort onto the jetties themselves, which honestly isn't the worst thing. Dirtier water close to the rocks has actually helped the bluefish bite; they don't mind a little chop pushing bait against structure.

Look ahead: tidal range keeps building right through the 12th, and if that pattern holds the way it usually does around here, expect the bass bite at current-driven spots like the Manasquan jetties and Shark River Inlet to get more consistent, not less. I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at first light, work the rock seams slow, and keep a bunker spoon rigged in case the blues show up uninvited — because lately, they have been.
